title: Sustained tail reduction via token-priority buckets and kernel-coordinated admission
creator: Aisha Kaplan
description: Reduce p99/p999 tail latency for continuous batching workloads by implementing token-level priority buckets coupled with a kernel-coordinated admission handshake. This work targets production inference paths that suffer from long tails when heterogeneous token lengths and attention routing cause suboptimal kernel selection and KV-cache misses.
rationale: Current continuous-batching admission treats requests as homogeneous leading to large variance in kernel execution time and sporadic KV cache warming. We observed recurring p99 spikes when a small fraction of long sequences or attention-heavy prompts entered batches and forced fallback kernels or large memory churn. A token-priority bucket approach lets us separate low-latency-friendly traffic from heavy attention work, while a light-weight kernel handshake lets the runtime choose the most appropriate kernel path and pre-warm caches before scheduling decode slots.
proposed_solution:
1) Admission: assign incoming requests into three token-priority buckets (fast, default, heavy) based on a cheap prefill estimator (prompt length, presence of attention tokens, recent model profiling signature).
2) Kernel handshake: extend the runtime admission protocol to include an optional kernel intent flag and KV-cache hint; when a heavy bucket request is admitted, the scheduler reserves a small warming window to prefetch KV slices or select a quantized kernel variant.
3) Deadline hedging: attach soft deadlines and token budgets so admission admits partial-prefill slots for heavy requests and allows decode to continue in a staged manner, minimizing blocking of fast bucket requests.
4) Batch shaping: enforce per-bucket shaping policies (max batch size, max wait) and enable cross-bucket gentle merging only when latency budgets permit.
5) Observability: emit per-bucket p50/p95/p99 and kernel-path histograms and compare unit-cost impact per route.
milestones: M1 - Spec and microbench plan (design doc + perf harness) - complete
M2 - Prototype admission buckets in staging runtime (+ trace events) - in progress
M3 - Kernel handshake API and lightweight KV prefetch implementation - blocked on kernel ABI review
M4 - A/B traffic experiment on canary fleet with real workload patterns - planned
M5 - Rollout with runtime feature flag and automated rollback SLOs - planned
acceptance_criteria: p99 latency on representative microburst workload reduced by >= 40% vs baseline
p999 latency reduced by >= 35% for the same workload
End-to-end throughput change <= 5% (no regression for dominant customers)
Kernel-path selection error rate < 1% after 24h of canary traffic
Observability dashboards show per-bucket metrics and automatic alerts for SLO regressions
testing_plan: Unit tests for bucket assignment heuristics and admission protocol
Microbench harness that replays observed tail patterns (long prompts, attention-heavy tokens) against q/kernel variants
Staging end-to-end: run mixed workload replay for 72h to validate p99 improvements and detect regressions
Canary A/B: 5% traffic on canary fleet, monitor p95/p99, kernel selection, and unit-cost for 48h
Chaos tests: simulate kernel fallback and slow KV-cache warming to validate graceful degradation
risks: Kernel ABI changes required by the handshake could delay rollout (blocked on PR review)
Misclassification of buckets can increase tail if heavy requests are erroneously merged into fast batches
KV prefetch increases memory pressure on GPUs leading to throughput impact if mis-tuned
Observability gaps may hide regressions without detailed per-kernel telemetry
